Business.title: Japan raises interest rate to new 31-year high to curb rising prices
Business.text:
Japan's central bank has raised its main interest rate to a fresh 31-year high as it continues to move away from decades of ultra-low borrowing costs and as the country faces increasing economic pressures.

In a widely expected move on Friday, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) increased the rate from 1% to 1.25% - a level not seen since 1995.

It comes as major central banks around the world are hiking rates as higher energy prices caused by the Iran war are helping to push up inflation.

On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in over three years, while the European Central Bank also increased its borrowing costs earlier this month.

The BOJ has been raising the rate since 2024, when it stood at minus 0.1%. It has now hiked rates six times in the last two and a half years.

Since then the bank has been steadily putting up the rate as it tries to reach a level similar to other major economies.

When a central bank raises rates, known as tightening monetary policy, the country's currency usually becomes stronger as it makes the it more attractive to traders.

"One of the world's last sources of ultra-cheap money is disappearing," said market analyst Lale Akoner from investment company eToro.

Japan is facing several economic challenges including a persistently weak yen, rising prices and a shrinking workforce.

Official figures published on Friday ahead of the BOJ announcement showed that inflation eased slightly last month.

Core inflation fell to 1.7% in August from 1.8% the previous month but remains close to the bank's 2% target level.

While Japan's inflation rate is not high by international standards, rising prices are a relatively new development in the economy.

Until recently the country had experienced very low inflation or deflation - falling prices - for around three decades.

Global oil and gas prices have risen this year as the Iran war caused major disruptions to shipments through the key Strait of Hormuz shipping route.

Japan is particularly vulnerable to those supply interruptions as it is heavily reliant on energy from the Middle East.

The country's currency has also been under pressure in recent months.

In August, Tokyo and Washington confirmed that they had jointly intervened to halt a slide in the yen after it fell to a fresh 40-year low.

The coordinated intervention was the first since 2011, when both countries took action together to weaken the yen after the devastating earthquake and tsunami that hit eastern Japan.

Both Japan's Ministry of Finance and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the time that they would not hesitate to conduct more joint interventions in the future.

Bessent has also been ramping up pressure on the BOJ to raise interest rates to help support the yen, calling on its Governor Kazuo Ueda to "do the right thing".

"If [the yen] remains weak despite higher rates, the resulting inflation pressure could force the BOJ to tighten faster than markets or Japan's government would like," Akoner said.

Business.title: Warren Buffett steps down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway after over 50 years
Business.text:
Warren Buffett is stepping down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway, the company that he took from a faltering textile manufacturer into a $1tn conglomerate over the course of 60 years.

Buffett’s son, Howard, 71, will take over as chair. Buffett, 96, cited his age as the main reason behind the transition, noting that he has a one-year-old great-grandchild who is “moving a bit faster than I am these days”.

“Serving as your chairman has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I have never taken your trust for granted,” Buffett, 96, said in a letter to shareholders. “Father Time always wins. He has, however, been generous with me. He has given me the opportunity to see Berkshire reach a point where I am more confident than ever about what lies ahead.”

Buffett said he will remain as chair emeritus and a director on the board. He left his post as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway in May 2025, shocking the audience of thousands at the company’s annual shareholder meeting in Omaha, Nebraska. Greg Abel, vice–chair of the company, replaced him as CEO.

Known as the “Oracle of Omaha”, Buffett built a reputation as a sharp-eyed investor, building up Berkshire Hathaway into a $1tn conglomerate. The company owns dozens of companies in construction, manufacturing, consumer goods and insurance, along with being a major investor in some of the biggest companies on the stock market, including Nvidia, Apple, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta.

Bloomberg places Buffett’s net worth at $145bn, making him the 10th richest person in the world.

Howard Buffett, known as “Howie”, is Buffett’s second child out of three and was long planned to be his father’s successor as chair of the company, having served on the board since 1993.

“He is getting it because he’s my son,” Buffett told the Wall Street Journal in January 2025. “I’m very, very, very lucky in the fact that I trust all three of my children.”

In a statement, Abel said that Buffett’s impact on the company “is without parallel in the history of American business”.

“The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian,” he said.

Business.title: Trump bans CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House
Business.text:
In his latest attack on the US constitution’s first amendment and the press, Donald Trump abruptly announced that he is banning outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House over their coverage.

In a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, the US president said he was expelling the news outlets “effective immediately” over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and threatened that bans for others outlets could follow.

He went on: “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

Trump defended the ban at an Oval Office event to promote his administration’s healthcare policies.

“I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox,” Trump told reporters, referring to friendly media outlets. “But what I do ask is just a semblance of truth.”

Reminded by one reporter that every president takes an oath to uphold the constitution, including the first amendment right to free speech, Trump said: “You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news.”

He added: “I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day. I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they’re going to write false stories all the time.”

Towards the end of a chaotic news conference, when a reporter asked Trump to explain how his ban on the three outlets would work, the president expressed confusion. “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban? Do you know how many bans I’m involved in?” Trump asked, seeming confused.

After another correspondent rephrased the question, asking, “What do you envision the bans would look like on the media outlets?”

Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?”

On Friday, the Washington Post reported that more American service members have died in the war on Iran than the Pentagon has publicly disclosed; CNN revealed that an “entirely false” intelligence report about a Chinese ship in the Middle East generated with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) had “almost started a war”; while a Politico report uncovered a Hill investigation after sensitive F-35 fighter jet technology unexpectedly made its way to Hong Kong, possibly giving China access to them.

Trump said his decision to ban the three outlets was unrelated to the stories. “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years,” he said, before threatening more media prohibitions could follow.

“There may be others to join them,” Trump said.

In a statement, a spokesperson for CNN said the network “stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting”.

“We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right,” the spokesperson said.

Politico said its reporters would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones”.

“We will vigorously defend our first amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” it added.

Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA), said the organization “stands in defense” of the banned reporters “who are being singled out for doing their jobs”.

“This is about more than the rights of journalists,” Henrich wrote in a statement. “It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.”

A spokesperson for MS Now declined to comment.

Trump’s move drew swift condemnation from Democrats and free speech groups. Chris Coons, a Democratic senator, wrote on social media: “Trump is once again trying to use the power of the presidency to punish a free press, now banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House. That is the behavior of an authoritarian, and we must defend the press’ right to hold those in power accountable.”

The White House press pool is a “public forum” under the first amendment, so the president cannot expel journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints, said Jameel Jaffer, executive director at Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University. To do so, would be “doubly unconstitutional”.

“The first amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage, just as it prohibits him from punishing universities because he doesn’t like the courses they offer, or from punishing law firms because he doesn’t like the clients they represent,” said Jaffer. “With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you’d think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now.”

Similarly, Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, said: “It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the first amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the ‘People’s House’ for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move.

“The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.”

Since returning to office, Trump has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major traditional news media at the White House, including the Associated Press, which was banned from press pool events in the Oval Office and on Air Force One after it continued to use Gulf of Mexico instead of Gulf of America in its coverage. The AP sued, and that case remains in litigation.

Trump’s White House also seized control over the organization of the presidential press pool, a rotation that determines which news organizations and reporters are allowed to follow – and question – the president in places such as the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One. The WHCA, an independent association made up of members of the media, traditionally coordinated rotating pool coverage of more than a dozen journalists allowed access to the president in smaller settings.

The Pentagon also attempted to introduce a new press policy to restrict the ability of journalists to gather and report on sensitive information, which culminated in a mass walkout of news media outlets who refused to sign the pledge. A federal judge later ruled the policy was unconstitutional.

The president has also launched high-profile legal battles with major outlets including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, CNN, ABC News and the BBC.

Sports.title: Chelsea analysis: No Joao Pedro, no goals as Xabi Alonso's problems mount
Sports.text:
Chelsea's problem was once again defending. But with striker Joao Pedro ruled out through injury, scoring goals also became an issue at Brentford on Friday.

The Brazilian striker's absence with a knee injury disrupted new manager Xabi Alonso's previously free-scoring attack, which featured Cole Palmer and club record £117m signing Morgan Rogers.

Danny Welbeck replaced the forward, but was unable to make an impact.

At Brentford, it was an even contest until Jaidon Anthony gave the hosts a 61st-minute lead - then Chelsea collapsed to a 3-0 defeat.

Early on this season, Chelsea were outscoring teams through the individual brilliance of their attack. Not now. And they have conceded 12 goals, more than any other side in the Premier League, albeit having played a game more than every other team.

Alonso is only the sixth manager to concede two or more goals in each of his first five Premier League matches in charge.

There is one conclusion to draw from that statistic: It is becoming increasingly urgent for Alonso to stop Chelsea from conceding. Some of his team's problems are inherited, but the new manager has not built any kind of tactical coherence in the opening weeks of the campaign.

Alonso has experimented with different systems, giving 11 debuts, including two on Friday - one for midfielder Mahdi Nicoll-Jazuli, the first 16-year-old to play for Chelsea in the Premier League, and one for new signing Jordan Henderson, 36, against his former club.

Ultimately, it was a tale of Chelsea's attack not firing, and the team then falling apart after Brentford got their noses in front. With the extended international break coming up, they have three weeks to stew on this latest defeat.

Chelsea signed a striker from Brighton for the second successive summer, bringing in Welbeck to reunite him with Joao Pedro and provide support in attack.

Welbeck, 35, was tidy in possession but, with little service, managed only 17 touches before being substituted in the 71st minute.

Unlike Joao Pedro, who is capable of creating chances for himself, Welbeck found it difficult to influence the game in the same way.

Joao Pedro came into the weekend with the most goal involvements in the Premier League, having scored three and provided three assists in four appearances this season.

His impact extends beyond goals and assists, with the Brazilian linking well with Palmer and Rogers. Against Brentford, however, Rogers arguably produced his quietest performance since arriving from Aston Villa in the summer.

Rogers eventually moved up front with fellow striker Emmanuel Emegha sidelined through injury and still waiting to make his Chelsea debut.

Before Brentford's opener, it was a closely contested match that appeared likely to be decided by the first goal. Chelsea, however, made victory a certainty for the hosts with a dramatic collapse.

Alonso has not managed to cure Chelsea's set-piece weaknesses. They have conceded 23 goals from set-pieces since the start of last season - no Premier League side has let in more. And Anthony's simple header from a corner took this season's total to five.

Set-piece defending was an area Chelsea sought to address when they appointed Bernardo Cueva from Brentford two years ago. This summer, he was replaced by another highly regarded specialist in Austin MacPhee.

Asked about Chelsea's defending from set-pieces, stand-in captain Levi Colwill told Sky Sports: "Not good enough. At times we have been bullied in the box and we definitely need to improve.

"We have full trust in our set-piece coach and are still adjusting to new ideas, but we need to improve as a team."

Like many of his predecessors, Alonso has been attempting to instil a stronger competitive edge within his squad and improve the mentality of his players.

That issue has often been linked to the relatively young age profile of the squad, but Chelsea fielded their oldest starting XI since May 2023. Henderson, in making his debut on Friday, lined up alongside fellow over-30s Welbeck and goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez.

"I would say that we have dropped our consistency and our competitive mentality in the second half. We know that small details can be decisive," Alonso said after Brentford added two late goals.

It is also fair to say Alonso is still experimenting with systems and personnel, and has yet to settle on a style of play that gives his side control throughout a match.

"It's not about looking for excuses," the Spaniard told Sky Sports. "We need to look at each other and know that we have to work and improve because there is still a long way to go."

After the initial excitement - and victories - provided by Alonso's attacking football, Chelsea head into the international break with serious questions to answer.

Sports.title: Athlos London: Keely Hodgkinson powers to victory in speed suit at all-female event
Sports.text:
Keely Hodgkinson powered to victory in a custom-made full-body speed suit before being presented with a Tiffany & Co crown as Athlos made its London debut.

Hodgkinson was greeted by loud cheers as she emerged on to a stage and revealed the all-black aerodynamic outfit at the third staging of the all-female athletics meet.

The 24-year-old ensured she ended a mixed year with a dominant 800m victory in front of a sellout home crowd at StoneX Stadium, bursting clear on the back straight and crossing the line in one minute 56.40 seconds.

Speaking about the outfit, Hodgkinson told BBC Sport: "This has been like a year in the making. It's a mixture of fashion and speed and science all coming together for maybe the future of athletics.

"It was a real honour for them to choose me to put this out first. We weren't sure when we were going to wear it.

"But an all-women's event that's all about the glitz and the glamour and putting eyes on women, a bit of a moment, I think was the perfect way to finish the season."

Created by Alexis Ohanian, Reddit co-founder and husband of tennis' 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams, Athlos was staging a meet for the first time outside of New York.

In addition to the silver Tiffany crown awarded to winners instead of medals, a top prize of $65,000 (£48,500) was on offer in each event.

The single-night meet included seven disciplines, each featuring six athletes, with money on offer for each position from a total event prize pot of $1.05m (£790,500).

American sprint stars Gabby Thomas and Sha'Carri Richardson were among the champions amid a party atmosphere which featured a live track-side DJ.

The athletes had arrived on a red carpet in north London but Hodgkinson saved her starring moment for the main event.

The eye-catching speed suit, reminiscent of that worn by Cathy Freeman in winning Olympic 400m gold in 2000, featured an open back and a hood with a ponytail opening - the latter, she said, was non-negotiable - while colour-changing 3D-printed nodes reduced drag in key areas.

Paired with dark sunglasses and Nike's latest carbon-plated spikes, it helped Hodgkinson achieve her first victory since the London Diamond League in July.

It has been a year of record-breaking highs and frustrating setbacks for the Olympic champion.

An indoor season in which she landed her first world 800m title and smashed a 24-year world record heightened expectations that she would take down the sport's longest-standing mark outdoors.

But a nasty fall suffered on a post-session cool down run in July, and a recurrence of the hamstring injury which kept her out of action for much of 2025 at the European Championships, conspired to hinder her progress.

While still improving her British record this summer, Hodgkinson finished second to breakout Swiss star Audrey Werro at both the European Championships and inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship.

However, with Swiss athlete Valentina Rosamilia finishing more than two seconds behind, she ended the season with a smile on her face and a crown on her head as she danced on stage with the night's other winners.

Ohanian has been clear about his eventual intention to make Athlos a global season-long league.

Athlos was supposed to expand to a two-day event in 2026, but the New York meeting scheduled for 2 October was cancelled following consultation with the athletes at the end of a long season.

Instead, Ohanian now hopes to align Athlos within the global athletics calendar from next year.

How that will work remains to be seen. The Diamond League, athletics' premier season-long series, runs from May until September, while the introduction of the Ultimate Championship - joining the Olympics and the World Championships on the calendar - means every season will now feature a global competition of some description.

American Masai Russell, who broke the 100m hurdles world record last month, was among the late Athlos withdrawals following last week's Ultimate, organised by the sport's governing body and offering record prize pot of $10m.

Athlos set out to be different, and it definitely felt that. There was as much showbusiness as there was sport - this was all about the "event".

Athletes arrived on bespoke London buses and walked the red carpet before their event. Several of the athletes said they enjoyed having the spotlight on them and being able to combine their sport with fashion and many will now be part of London Fashion Week.

Georgia Hunter Bell emerged from a melee of screaming children telling her she was their idol onto the red carpet and said she felt "valued".

It was certainly noisy, and the resident DJ meant at times it felt more like you were in a club than an athletics meet. But the athletes and fans seemed to buy into the vibe.

One man told me he had been to 27 world championships and five Olympics and wasn't sure he'd enjoy Athlos, but loved it. A woman whose daughter is part of the athletics club who train at StoneX Stadium said she thought it was "remarkable" and "inspirational".

There will be learnings from this first trip to London, but as a starting point, it felt like it lived up to its hype.

Sports.title: World Series of Darts Finals 2026: Luke Littler survives scare to progress
Sports.text:
World number one Luke Littler survived a first-round scare to overcome Danny Noppert in a thrilling World Series of Darts Finals match in Amsterdam.

The 19-year-old, seeking his second World Series Finals victory after 2024, recently whitewashed the Dutchman, who is a former UK Open champion, 6-0 on his way to winning the Czech Darts Open.

There would be no repeat here as Noppert won three straight legs to take a 3-1 lead.

Having levelled the match at 3-3, Littler turned to the crowd and tapped his ears in response to boos.

Despite the teenager then busting his score, Noppert failed to take advantage and retake the lead.

With the score 4-4, Littler let out a passionate roar towards the crowd after a wonderful 95 checkout, with Noppert left on 46. The finish brought him within one leg of victory, which he comfortably secured.

Littler will now face fellow Englishman Nathan Aspinall, who defeated Raymond Smith 6-4.

Wales' Gerwyn Price beat Brody Klinge 6-4 to progress, but was made to work after taking control at 5-0.

Klinge avoided a whitewash and then grew in confidence, turning what once looked like a thrashing into a one-leg deficit.

However, Price comfortably closed out the match and will now face Jim Long.

Motomu Sakai beat England's Callan Rydz 6-5 to progress, while James Wade overcame Damon Heta 6-5.

Wales' Jonny Clayton will face Sakai after he beat Maik Kuivenhoven 6-3.

Sports.title: BMW PGA Championship: Rory McIlroy in contention at Wentworth
Sports.text:
BMW PGA Championship - round two

-12 R Gerard (US); -10 A Scott (Aus), F Celli (Ita); -9 M Elvira (Spa), A Rai (Eng)

Selected others: -8 R Fox (NZ), R Fisher (Eng), R McIlroy (NI), I Elvira (Spa), JJ Spaun (US); -7 M Wallace (Eng); -6 S Straka (Aut), A Noren (Swe); -5 L Aberg (Swe), V Hovland (Nor); -4 D Law (Sco), R MacIntyre (Sco), S Lowry (Ire), M Fitzpatrick (Eng); -3 J Rose (Eng)

Rory McIlroy stayed in contention with a five-under 67 to sit four strokes behind second-round leader Ryan Gerard at the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth.

The Northern Irishman made three birdies in his opening five holes and recovered from dropped shots on the eighth and 16th by picking up four strokes on the back nine, including birdies on the 17th and 18th holes.

Reigning Masters champion McIlroy's hopes of winning a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title were also buoyed by the withdrawal of Patrick Reed after nine holes.

The American, who currently leads the standings on the DP World Tour, had been well placed after the first round but was forced to retire through injury while nine-over par for Friday's round.

"Unfortunately he's pulled out this week, which gives me an opportunity to try to claw back some ground that I lost last week in Ireland," said McIlroy, who is at eight under overall.

"This weekend is a big weekend for me to pick up a few points and make the race even tighter going into these last few weeks. I'm in a great spot heading into the weekend."

Gerard made five birdies and an eagle in a flawless round of 65 to leave him two shots clear of Australia's Adam Scott and Italian Filippo Celli, who are at 10 under.

US PGA Championship winner Aaron Rai, who played alongside McIlroy and Open champion Ryan Fox in a marquee group, also enjoyed a birdie-birdie finish as he signed for a 69.

The Englishman, who had shared the lead overnight, was at nine under alongside Spain's Manuel Elvira, with McIlroy and Fox among a quintet of players a further shot back.

Five-time major champion Brooks Koepka was among the big names to miss the cut at one over.

Englishman Tommy Fleetwood will also miss the weekend after a 74 left him at three over, while Spain's Jon Rahm endured another day to forget, following up a six-over-par 78 on Thursday with a 77 to end 138th and last of all those to finish on Friday.

Sports.title: Brentford vs Chelsea player ratings: Henderson a vocal leader as Thiago lifts weight off shoulders
Sports.text:
Caoimhin Kelleher: An accomplished display, although he was never required to make any outstanding saves. 6

Michael Kayode: Played a couple of sloppy passes and rarely ventured forward. 6

Kristoffer Ajer: A sizeable presence at the back despite coming under significant pressure from crosses in open play and from set-pieces. 7

Jannik Schuster: The young defender excelled in his own box but looked nervous in possession on a few occasions, including an overhit backpass that could have led to an own goal. He then set up the winner. 7

Keane Lewis-Potter: A poor clearance led to a Neto chance in the 10th minute, but he was impressive on the counter-attack. That perhaps owed something to his experience of learning the left-back role after previously playing as an attacker. 6

Yehor Yarmoliuk: On his 100th appearance, he threatened with a powerful long-range effort in the 37th minute and created Brentford's best chance shortly after half-time. 7

Vitaly Janelt: Did just enough to halt a Cole Palmer dribble early on, although he risked conceding a penalty. He provided a physical presence in midfield, with a potential Germany debut on the horizon under new manager Jurgen Klopp. 7

Mikkel Damsgaard: The Dane was not at his usual level from set-pieces or with his shooting from distance until he delivered an incredible whipped corner that led to the opening goal. 6

Kevin Schade: The in-form forward produced several pressure-relieving dribbles and had a shot blocked in the first half. Played a part in the final two goals. 7

Igor Thiago: The Brazil international was on a four-game goalless run before kick-off and worked hard but struggled in front of goal. He eventually delivered with a late strike to seal victory and his celebration looked like a weight then lifted off his shoulders, along with his Brentford shirt. 7

Jaidon Anthony: After a quiet first half, he missed his side's best chance early in the second half but responded well to score the opener. 7

Pedro Neto: His well-struck effort was saved in the 10th minute. He was lively throughout, linking up well in attack and stretching Brentford with his pace. 6

Jordan Henderson: There were no signs of rust. After receiving some early boos, he settled into the game and looked a vocal leader on the pitch. He also put some good corners into the box. 7

Sports.title: Max Dowman: Arsenal open to loan switch for teenage prodigy in right circumstances
Sports.text:
Arsenal are open to allowing teenage prodigy Max Dowman to leave the club on loan this term if it aids his development.

Last season, the 16-year-old set two records, as the youngest player to score in Premier League history and for the Gunners.

However, while he is yet to feature in the English top flight this term, he marked his first appearance of the season with two goals in Arsenal's 4-2 win at Ipswich in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday.

And while his manager Mikel Arteta stressed that he is keen to keep the youngster involved in his senior squad, he said the club will evaluate what is best for Dowman at regular intervals.

"We will evaluate every six months where we are and what is the best thing for him to do and then make the right decision," Arteta said.

"It depends on a lot of factors. What he needs, and what the team needs as well, the availability we have in the squad, the minutes that he is playing and the qualities of those minutes.

"We have to be open, but now the focus is to be here and to impact the team."

Dowman, who completed his GCSEs in the summer, will be eligible to make a loan move when he turns 17 on 31 December.

The winter transfer window is scheduled to open the following day, with League One side Luton's manager Jack Wilshere, the former Arsenal midfielder, believed to have expressed an interest in taking the youngster on loan.

"We haven't really listened to any of the possibilities because we were crystal clear that we wanted to have Max in the squad, that we wanted him to be part of the pre-season and then start to see where we are from there," Arteta added.

Dowman featured 13 times for Arsenal last term as they ended their 22-year wait to win the Premier League.

And with Arteta keen to protect the teenager, he was guarded around whether it may be too early to send Dowman out on loan.

"There have been many cases of that age when they have gone out and been successful and others not," Arteta added.

"In my particular case, I was 17 when I went to Paris [St-Germain]. It depends on the atmosphere that you find there, and how much the coach believes in you as to whether you go there just to be part of a squad or play minutes.

"Which country, it depends. But now he is in a good place, let's keep him here."

Starting by defeating Manchester City in the Community Shield, the Gunners have won all seven of their domestic and European fixtures this term.

And Dowman will hope that his performance against the Tractor Boys puts him into Arteta's thinking for Saturday's Premier League trip to Brighton.

"The best way to knock on the door is to do it on the pitch, not in the office," added Arteta when asked about Dowman's prospects of featuring against the Seagulls.

"Then you just leave out the arguments. When a player delivers constantly on the pitch, every single day in training, that's the best way, that's the best signal for the manager. That's the best signal for his team-mates, too.

"And what Max did the other day, alongside all the other players as well that haven't played many minutes this season, was really impressive."

Sports.title: WXV Global Series: Inspired Wales stun South Africa in eight-try demolition
Sports.text:
Tries: Keight, Tuipulotu 2, Lockwood, Davies, K Jones, Neumann, Callender Cons: Bell 5

South Africa (5) 19

Tries: Jacobs, Tshiremba, Samboya Cons: Dolf 2

Wales returned to winning ways in emphatic fashion with an eight-try victory over South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park.

The hosts had gone nine Tests without a victory heading into their WXV Global Series opener, with a tight contest predicted against a Springboks side ranked three places above them in the world.

But Sean Lynn's bold selections paid off as Wales attacked with a freedom and intent they have not produced for years.

They were six tries to the good in a dominant first half, with the visitors made to pay for indiscipline.

Tighthead Sisilia Tuipulotu was back to her irrestistible best, scoring in either half, while co-captain Alex Callender returned from injury with a typically impressive player-of-the-match display.

Lynn had told his players to be brave in the build-up, and he was courageous with his team selection after moving scrum-half Keira Bevan to 10.

The gamble paid off as the hosts enjoyed a perfect start under Friday night lights and it was fitting that the recently crowned Welsh Rugby Writers' player of the year Courtney Keight bagged the opening score.

Georgia Evans and Tuipulotu had made the hard yards before the ball was spread wide to Keight on the left wing and she cut inside to go over.

Kelsey Jones' turnover provided the launchpad for the second, with Evans popping a neat ball back inside for Tuipulotu to charge to the line.

South Africa responded with Felicia Jacobs benefiting from a dominant scrum on Wales' five-metre line, but that was to be their only score in a one-sided half.

Former Cardiff City footballer Amy Williams came within metres of scoring after winning the footrace to Lisa Neumann's grubber kick, but Seren Lockwood was first to the breakdown and darted over herself.

It was a double blow for the visitors who had hooker Lindelwa Gwala sent to the sin bin for being offside in the build-up.

Wales took full advantage with Maisie Davies showing her power to score her first international try and secure Wales' bonus point.

The hosts were in dreamland, but had to revert to their usual half-back pairing when Lockwood failed to return from a head injury assessment, with Bevan going back to scrum-half and Lleucu George slotting in at 10.

The enforced changes did little to halt Wales' flow with Freya Bell coming agonisingly close from a five-metre driving lineout, but Jones was there to clean up as she crossed over.

South Africa then went down to 13, with lock Danelle Lochner sent to the sin bin for a high tackle on Kate Williams, a card that would later be upgraded to a 20-minute red.

That paved the way for the pick of Wales' first-half tries. A solid scrum provided the platform for the ball to be worked out wide to Neumann who cruised over from her new full-back position.

It was Wales at their clinical best as they headed down the tunnel 38-5 in front.

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
Sports.text:
Chelsea have not won this west London derby since Brentford’s first Premier League season. Each visit since October 2021’s 1-0 win, Ben Chilwell the scorer, has been a draw. This season has continued the divergence between the clubs’ respective approaches, Brentford’s solidity and continuity contrasting with Chelsea attempting their latest reboot. Kevin Schade, after two well-taken goals at Bournemouth, will fancy facing a defence not yet attuned to Xabi Alonso’s configurations. Only one team has won a Premier League title with a defensive trio: Chelsea’s last title team, in 2016-17 under Antonio Conte. Alonso’s attack has been rather more successful, presenting another challenge for Jannik Schuster. Replacing Nathan Collins, the 20-year-old central defender had a tough examination from Bournemouth’s Evanilson on his first Premier League start, emerging with credit. For Chelsea, João Pedro has three goals and three assists, but doubts surrounding his fitness could lead to Danny Welbeck’s first league start. John Brewin

What happens when a very stoppable force meets an extremely movable object? We will be tuning into events at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday to find out as 19th-placed Aston Villa arrive in north London. The teams have scored one goal between them in the league and are desperately hoping for a first Premier League win. The return of Pedro Porro is big for Roberto De Zerbi and that should bring the Archie Gray Experiment at right-back to a merciful end. No Premier League starting XI feels less settled than Spurs – most players look as if they are a mistake or two from being dropped – which has culminated in a side that seems governed by fear and continuously prefers to take the safe option. After coming off the bench against Everton and Liverpool in the past week, the injury-plagued James Maddison will be itching to start and take some sort of initiative for Tottenham. Michael Butler

When Fabian Hürzeler spoke about Brighton’s success being founded on them being “well structured” after their stirring comeback against Manchester United at Old Trafford on Wednesday, he could have been referring to Malick Yalcouyé. The 20-year-old Ivorian moved to the south coast in 2024 after spending just a few months with IFK Gothenburg in Sweden but had to wait until this season to make his senior debut for Brighton after being sent on loan to Sturm Graz in Austria and then Swansea last season. With Jack Hinshelwood sidelined by injury until after the international break, Yalcouyé has taken his chance in the No 10 role and already found the net twice in the Premier League as Brighton have made a brilliant start. Arsenal are up next for the division’s top scorers – who have 13 goals from their opening four matches – and Mikel Arteta should be wary of the threat posed by Yalcouyé and co as the champions prepare for a fourth away game in succession. Ed Aarons

Vitalii Mykolenko’s early-season improvement has gone largely unheralded – and it probably always will be among his detractors – but at a time when David Moyes needs experienced players to step up and defy the constraints of a small squad, the Everton left-back has produced. Having signed a new three-year contract in the summer, and seemingly bulked up, the Ukraine international has kept his critics quiet with several impressive displays for a defence that has four clean sheets in six matches. There remains a problematic lack of cover at left-back after the decision to loan Adam Aznou to Málaga for the season but Mykolenko, the better defender, has eased the concerns that surrounded his position before the new campaign. Ipswich’s new forward recruits, Emersonn and Zian Flemming, will test Everton’s solidity but Moyes’s side will have made an encouraging start should they sign off with a win before the extended international break. Andy Hunter

As befits a lover of direct football, Matthias Jaissle likes to get straight to the point. On Thursday he was asked whether, in the light of Monday night’s 4-1 thrashing at Leeds and a raft of injuries, he was tempted to perhaps switch to a back five or modify his beloved “vertical” approach when Hull visit Tyneside on Saturday. The reply proved unequivocal. “No,” said a manager unafraid to answer questions with a single word. Instead Jaissle expects his young team to retain faith in a wider vision as Newcastle – who signed eight players aged 24 and under this summer – adapt to life after Bruno Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon. “It’s a brave journey the club is going on and I’m fully committed in that,” the German said. “If there’s one setback, we shouldn’t delete our journey or our vision. We’re fully committed. We’re fully aligned. We anticipated that something like that against Leeds would happen. It’s on us to respond. But while still believing. We don’t change.” Louise Taylor

Many scoffed at the £45m that was paid for Liam Delap in the summer but Nottingham Forest feels like the perfect place for the striker to regain his form. Forest previously thrived with the now injured Chris Wood as their arrowhead and Delap is something of a younger regent for the New Zealander – powerful, instinctive and willing to bring others into play. During Saturday’s win at Villa, Morgan Gibbs-White and Delap looked as if they already have an understanding and both will be keen to capitalise against a Coventry side that have conceded eight goals in the past two games. After a nervy campaign last season, Forest feel back in the ascendancy and will have been delighted that plans to increase the City Ground’s capacity from 31,000 to 52,500, at an estimated cost of £790m, were approved by the local council on Wednesday. MB

After watching Bournemouth make their European bow from afar in San Sebastián, a city Andoni Iraola knows inside out, the Basque head coach will return to his previous club on Sunday. Iraola – whose assistants Tommy Elphick and Shaun Cooper played for Bournemouth, the former captaining the club into the Premier League in 2015 – led the Dorset club into the Europa League by recording their best-ever finish, sixth. His body of work on the south coast earned him the Liverpool opportunity and a warm welcome is a guarantee. Despite the Cherries’ slow start under Iraola’s successor, Marco Rose, they will pose tricky opposition. The German spent a couple of hours in Iraola’s company before officially starting in June and both will be braced for an all-action contest. Eddie Howe failed to beat Bournemouth in the eight league games he managed against them with Newcastle and Iraola and his staff will expect a tough test. Ben Fisher

Dominic Calvert-Lewin will be a man on a mission against Crystal Palace at Elland Road on Saturday. Daniel Farke’s centre-forward hopes to become the first Leeds player to score in six consecutive home league games since Arthur Hydes back in 1932. Managers often, quite rightly, say players matter more than formations but, in Calvert-Lewin’s case, Farke’s switch to 3-5-2 late last November proved a road to Damascus moment. Until then he had struggled as the team’s lone striker but, once he was paired with Noah Okafor or Lukas Nmecha, the goals started to flow. Granted, Leeds sometimes play 3-4-3 or, occasionally, revert to a back four but Calvert-Lewin has emphasised the importance of attacking partnerships. After collecting eight points from their opening four games, Farke’s team have registered the best beginning to a top-tier campaign of any Leeds team since David O’Leary’s class of 2001-02. Will it continue at Palace’s expense? Is Hydes’ record under threat? Might 3-5-2 be the answer to ending more strikers’ goal droughts? Louise Taylor

Manchester City’s maximum 12 points from their first four Premier League games featured 1-0 wins (over Coventry and Manchester United), a 2-1 victory (Bournemouth), and a 4-1 success (Crystal Palace). Conceding only two goals while scoring eight is an impressive record that is only marginally bettered by the champions, Arsenal (one conceded, eight scored in their 12-point tally), and it seems a rosy augury that Enzo Maresca’s team will be genuine title contenders this season. Régis Le Bris, though, plots to halt City’s perfect start, and can draw on guiding Sunderland to a share of the points last season against the FA Cup holders, though that was at the Stadium of Light. In the corresponding fixture at the Etihad Stadium, City cruised to a 3-0 win. Jamie Jackson

Sports.title: Alex Ovechkin claims he’s ‘not in politics’. His pro-Putin video says the opposite
Sports.text:
When Russian launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, reporters asked Washington Capitals captain Alexander Ovechkin for his thoughts. It was no secret, even then, that Ovechkin was close to Vladimir Putin. Years before, Ovechkin boosted the Russian president in a social media campaign and featured Putin in his own Instagram profile photo. “He is my president,” Ovechkin said of Putin shortly after the invasion. “But [like] I said, I’m not in politics, I’m an athlete.” That’s over. He’s in politics now.

“The thing about the video: I’m Russian,” Ovechkin told reporters Thursday. The video in question is one he taped for United Russia, a group supporting Putin, ahead of parliamentary elections. Ovechkin appears in the video alongside Sergei Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, Margarita Simonyan, the editor-in-chief of the state-controlled media outlet RT, and others. “I’m for peace and love, and I hope, in the world, it doesn’t matter who you are,” Ovechkin told reporters. “I hope everybody understands everybody wants peace, and everybody hope everything’s going to be OK in the world.”

A day before, the Capitals released a statement that lauded Ovechkin and treated his video participation in the same mundane, neutral tone. “Alex Ovechkin is a Russian citizen who lives in Moscow with his family during the offseason and will live there following his retirement. This summer, while in Russia, he was asked by his country to participate in a video campaign,” the team said. “As the longest-tenured athlete in Washington, DC and a pillar of the community, his focus and ours is on the season ahead and the continued impact he makes on the ice and in our city.”

It’s undeniable that Ovechkin has had an impact on DC during his long NHL career, never playing anywhere else, bringing the Capitals their first and only Stanley Cup and becoming the sport’s greatest goalscorer. But now that Ovechkin is also into politics – by choice – it’s fair to start asking what the impact of those politics is, too, even if he doesn’t want to talk about it.

In an awkward bit of timing, in an indictment unsealed Tuesday, US federal prosecutors accused five men of being part of a network planning to assassinate Russian dissidents and others on US soil, including one who reportedly lived in Washington. Just one concrete example of the Putin government in action – its continued impact, if you like – right in Ovechkin’s adopted home town. Elsewhere, on X, former NHL goaltender Dominik Hasek – a Czech icon who has been an outspoken Putin critic for years – tore into the Capitals’ statement on Ovechkin for turning a blind eye to the impact of that politics in Europe. “This statement ignores the hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of Ukrainians and Russians killed or maimed – casualties for which Ovechkin bears a significant share of responsibility through his public stance,” Hasek wrote.

A “significant” share may be stretching it, but Hasek’s broader point is that there ought to be a reckoning here, that the people involved should take ownership. For Ovechkin, that would probably mean repeating the message that he supported as publicly in the US as he does in Russia, instead of distancing himself from it the moment it becomes uncomfortable and offering “peace and love”. For the Capitals, taking a moral stand could mean anything from making a donation to a Ukrainian charity to stripping Ovechkin of his captaincy, to barring him from playing.

But that would mean the organization would have to have the guts to address it as more than an uncomfortable topic to be endured just long enough to look like anyone cared, which is also what happened Thursday in the media scrum. After answering a couple of questions about the United Russia video, Ovechkin pivoted. “All right,” he said, “let’s do hockey questions.” “Happy birthday,” one reporter said almost immediately, ushering back the illusion of normalcy. “Did you get a cake?” Ovechkin replied he is on a diet. Everyone laughed. No one in the scrum made him answer for anything. When an ESPN reporter pressed him later with questions on the video and the invasion, Ovechkin said he is “not in politics” and “can’t say who’s right and who’s wrong” before abruptly ending the interview.

Fans are now left to figure out an unwindable ethical quandary that was never theirs to solve. If you keep watching or keep wearing your Ovechkin jersey, you’re liable to be accused of tacitly supporting a repressive regime; if you choose to boycott, you’re accused of “politicizing” sports. The fans are left holding the bag, searching for accountability, while those responsible for it walk away behind a mealy mouthed word cloud.

Sports.title: Jon Rahm shoots 78-77 and slumps off in last place at PGA Championship
Sports.text:
Missed cuts for Tommy Fleetwood and Jon Rahm at the PGA Championship would be notable enough even without contemplating the latter’s 36-hole score.

The sight of Rahm dead last was remarkable – after rounds of 78 and 77, he was 11 over par. Fleetwood’s exit at plus three, while less dramatic, was another obvious blow to the tournament organisers at Wentworth. On a day of high-profile departures, injury forced Patrick Reed out of the event midway through his round. That scenario might have repercussions as Rory McIlroy seeks to prise the DP World Tour’s order of merit from the American’s grasp.

Rahm did not stop for media duties but may have offered extenuating circumstance. It is just that seeing a player of such status and talent toil so badly turns heads. The Spaniard is awaiting the imminent arrival of his fourth child, a matter to which he referred before a ball was struck in Surrey.

The LIV backdrop also cannot be ignored; Rahm is fully expected to depart the ailing circuit when the formalities of a voluntary bankruptcy filing are completed. This is, however, a situation now in the hands of the courts. It would be perfectly natural if Rahm finds himself unable to appropriately focus when inside the ropes. Two Wentworth rounds involved three birdies, 10 bogeys and two double bogeys.

Fleetwood needed a change of fortune, albeit not a significant one, after Thursday’s 73. The 15th has proved his nemesis this week, with a bogey five during the first round followed up by a double bogey on day two. Despite delivering three birdies, the 35-year-old slipped to a 74.

Reed – who looked a candidate to win after the first round – played his first nine holes in 44, nine over par. He grasped his left wrist after a pulled tee shot on the 10th, before his withdrawal was confirmed and he headed straight for medical treatment.

Elements of normality were provided by Adam Scott, who is seeking to become the oldest winner of this event. The 46-year-old Australian backed up a 67 with an identical score. Scott would place huge stock in a Wentworth win.

“Let’s put the majors aside for a minute,” he said. “I think there’s the Players Championship, Wentworth and the Australian Open for me at that level of importance. So it would mean a lot? Absolutely. I mean, it would be huge.

“I’m not heaping pressure on myself to go and win this tournament. I feel like at this point I just need to put my head into a place where I can enjoy the next couple of days. I have done this many times in the past, not so much lately, but I think hopefully that kind of instinct and memory comes back in this position. If I can enjoy myself the next couple of days, I think I’ll get the best out of myself.”

Scott will form part of an International team trying to end a miserable run against the United States in the Presidents Cup. The event takes place next weekend at Medinah. Scott and Ryan Fox, the Open champion, will fly straight to Illinois from this tournament.

Not part of the Presidents Cup equation is JJ Spaun, which has left the American somewhat miffed. Spaun’s 66 here moved him to eight under and he made his shock at being omitted from Brandt Snedeker’s team plain.

“It was disappointing to be left off,” the winner of last year’s US Open said. “I wasn’t expecting it, to be honest. I kind of hung my hat on my experience with the Ryder Cup last year. I made it to the Tour Championship this year. I won in San Antonio. I did everything I could. I was the odd man out.”

Sports.title: Josh Allen shines again as Bills celebrate new home with slugfest victory over Lions
Sports.text:
Josh Allen quickly put his stamp on the Buffalo Bills’ new stadium, which has been dubbed “The House that Allen built.”

Allen threw three touchdown passes and ran for two scores, and the Bills beat the Detroit Lions 41-31 on Thursday night in the first regular-season game at Highmark Stadium.

It was Allen’s fourth five-TD outing, and followed a four-touchdown outing (two passing, two rushing) in Buffalo’s season-opening win at Houston.

“[We won in a] short week against a really good team who kept us fighting until the last second there,” Allen said after the game.

Allen followed the pregame fireworks celebration with more of his own by overseeing touchdown drives on each of Buffalo’s first four possessions.

He scored the first regular-season TD in the stadium on a one-yard run 5:51 into the opening quarter. He followed that with a 43-yard scoring pass to a wide-open Josh Palmer. Tight ends Dalton Kincaid, with a 16-yard catch, and Dawson Knox, with a one-yarder, also scored for Buffalo in the first half.

Allen finished the night 20 of 31 for 248 yards, and added 72 yards rushing. James Cook had 134 yards rushing and put the game away with a one-yard TD run late in the fourth quarter.

“I got a little emotional during the national anthem, feeling super blessed and lucky to do what I do. This is a great spot, we’re going to be here for a long time, hopefully the fans enjoyed it,” said Allen.

Allen’s two rushing TDs upped his career total to 83, moving him into a tie for 18th on the NFL list with Jim Taylor. He also picked up his 90th regular-season victory, becoming one of just four quarterbacks to reach that milestone through their first nine seasons.

The Lions were undone by their injury-depleted defense, and a banged-up offensive line that had difficulty opening holes for Jahmyr Gibbs and protecting Jared Goff.

After rallying from a 21-0 deficit to cut Buffalo’s lead to 34-24, the Lions offense stalled midway through the fourth quarter. Backed up at their own 10, the Lions went three-and-out and were forced to punt after Goff had two passes tipped by Deone Walker, and Gibbs was stopped for no gain.

Goff finished 26 of 38 for 327 yards and four touchdowns. Amon-Ra St Brown had nine catches for 142 yards and two scores. Gibbs also scored on an 11-yard catch but was limited to 52 yards rushing. Sam LaPorta scored on a one-yard catch.

The Lions’ defense got off to a dreadful start, allowing the Bills to score 27 points and gain 299 yards in the first half alone. The struggles carried over from a season-opening 31-30 overtime win over New Orleans, in which the Saints rallied from a 21-0 first-half deficit and lost only after their two-point conversion failed in overtime.

The Lions’ troubles began on Buffalo’s second drive when two defenders converged on DJ Moore, allowing Allen to find Palmer wide open deep for a 43-yard touchdown. On Buffalo’s next drive, a holding penalty against Rock Ya-Sin, negated Skyler Gill-Howard’s interception of a tipped pass.

The Lions’ offense had its own sputters, with Goff sacked twice and also having a snap go over his head on Detroit’s first two series.

The $2.1bn Highmark Stadium that officially opened last month was built across the street from the Bills’ former home. The new stadium has a capacity of just over 60,000, about 12,000 less than the old facility. What’s different is the layout, with the new facility’s seating structure built steeper, placing viewers more on top of the action. The new building also features a canopy, which helps project crowd noise directly on to field.

Bills fans began arriving two and three days earlier, with a private lot nearly filled with RVs by Tuesday.

Gaming_Tech.title: Flight chaos caused by millisecond software defect, says air traffic control body
Gaming_Tech.text:
An air traffic control failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect"affectingthe system underpinning UK air space management, the national air traffic service Nats has said.

The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data.

The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas.

Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe told the BBC he would not resign, saying the software defect was "very, very obscure."

"You can fly to almost anywhere from almost any airport at almost any time. If that stops, even for a moment, then you get huge disruption.

"My job is to make sure that we have this happen as infrequently as possible," he added.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption "completely unacceptable", while industry body Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for costs incurred.

The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of Mr Rolfe.

There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines, and about the fact that they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the regulator judges the situation was extraordinary circumstances.

In an initial report, external, Nats said the software defect meant air traffic controllers had reduced information available, so restrictions were put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety.

The defect occurred at 10:00am on 8 September, but it did not become apparent this was a serious problem for another two and a half hours.

The system restart did not start until just after 3:15pm, and restrictions on UK airspace were not lifted until 7:30pm.

Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.

The disruption took days to completely resolve because of the number of planes and crew left out of place.

Mr Rolfe apologised to those affected by the disruption, saying Nats was "devastated".

"However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question."

Nats has "tested these systems so much," he added.

"We spent so much time making sure they work that anything that does happen of this nature is, by its very nature, going to be incredibly complicated and probably difficult to understand at the time," he said.

Reacting to the Nats report, the transport secretary described the disruption as "completely unacceptable" and "frustrating" for passengers, airlines and airports.

"It's clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos," Alexander said, adding that a Civil Aviation Authority review was underway.

This is the third national air traffic incident in the past three years.

In 2023, a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday weekend caused chaos for 700,000 passengers.

There was another, smaller Nats outage in 2025, which caused 150 cancellations.

Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said: "Once again, it is passengers who have suffered and airlines who have picked up the pieces - and the tab - of an ATC [Air Traffic Control] system failure, while Nats itself faces no real consequences."

He added that passengers deserved "commitment and proof that the system is being fixed".

Alderslade also said Airlines UK was writing to NATS "to demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience."

Gaming_Tech.title: Robotics: Firms race to improve robot training systems
Gaming_Tech.text:
Freddo the robot walks across the office and takes a plastic bottled offered by a staff member.

Given that a robot recently beat Usain Bolt's 100m sprint record, it's not the most startling achievement.

But the speed by which Freddo has been trained to walk, recognise the bottle and grasp it is impressive. It took just a few minutes to develop those skills and upload them to Freddo. His developers say rival systems could take days to attain such skills.

I'm at Vsim, a British start-up based in Cambridge. Founders Michelle Lu and Kier Storey hope one day their software will control robots that can navigate and do useful tasks in the home and workplace.

But there's a long way to go.

"It's a weird situation with robotics because actually the stuff that we find as humans to be incredibly difficult, like gymnastics, you can get robots to do reasonably well. The stuff that humans are really good at, like fine dexterity, is really hard in robots," Storey says.

Freddo's skills were honed in a virtual environment, where a task can be performed in a computer simulation millions of times. Once the optimum solution (known as a policy) is found, it can be uploaded and used by the hardware - in this case Freddo.

Such virtual simulations are a common way to train robots. Tech giant Nvidia has a system called Isaac Sim which works that way - Lu and Storey both worked on an early version of it.

In 2022 they decided to set up Vsim, to build the their own training system environment and other tools.

As they were starting from scratch Lu and Storey could optimise the software to exploit the powerful computer chips used in AI, known as graphics processing units or GPUs.

"The underlying algorithms that we were using for most of these robotic simulations they hark back to the 1970s and 1980s, but those algorithms are not really brilliant fits for GPUs," Storey says.

Within months they realised their system could work much faster than anything they had seen before.

"Eighteen months in and we actually have a completely functional, super high-performance simulator," says Lu.

The software is so efficient that it can run on the hardware carried by Freddo. That means the robot can run tens of thousand of simulations while it is moving around.

"It can look about a second, or so, ahead into the future for 20,000 different kind of combinations of things that might happen," Storey explains.

And that would be vital for a robot moving around an unstructured environment like the average home.

"Things outside of the robot's control, like humans, animals or even other robots, could do things that require a change of strategy. These unexpected events could happen very quickly and the robot needs to be able to quickly adapt to ensure its actions remain safe and on-mission," Lu says.

Vsim is a start-up with 10 engineers working on its tech. Nvidia is at the other end of the industry. It dominates the market for computer chips used for AI and has a leading robotics software division, with hundreds of engineers.

It does not build robots, instead it has a suite of software designed to let organisations train and control robots.

That includes virtual simulation training systems and a so-called world model, external, called Cosmos, which gives a robot an understanding of the physics of the real world and how its environment might change as it moves around.

But even with the powerful computer resources available to Nvidia, the software only gives a rudimentary understanding of the real world.

"Manipulation, - where I just grab a bottle, that's not too hard. The problem is when you start doing long-horizon tasks, where I say: 'I want you to take the bottle and I want you to fill it up and I want you to go pour'," says Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at Nvidia.

But he's confident that good progress is being made. This year Nvidia has started using AI agents to help build virtual environments to train robots and validate whether the solutions from training work or not.

"When we talk about creating the [virtual] world and actually scanning it in - a lot of that is actually manual labour.

"We're just throwing agents at it... it's basically given us a huge workforce," Huang says.

Simulation is not the only method for training robots. They can also be trained by watching human or video demonstrations.

Rika Antonova has been working in the field of robotics since 2015 and is currently an associate professor at the Department of Computer Science and Technology at the University of Cambridge.

Her research is focused on, external developing software and hardware that can aid robots to learn complex behaviour.

Antonova works with a training system called MuJoCo, owned by Google's DeepMind since 2021. It's open-source software, which means researchers can use it for free, and are allowed to tinker with the code.

"It is very, very user-friendly. So for research groups or for small start-ups, that's useful," she says.

She says that Vsim's approach - very fast simulation - is promising.

"If you have a very, very fast simulator, then you can simulate hundreds of millions of samples in that few seconds that your robot is thinking about how to adjust its motion, and then you can change the motion almost in real time," she says.

But those simulated environments are still rough approximations of the real world, which limits what can be trained.

"There are certain things that are hard to model in simulation, like highly deformable objects and cutting," she says.

It's a challenge that Nvidia and Lu and Storey at Vsim are working on.

Lu says their system has "reduced approximation, using accurate simulations to train models that genuinely work in reality as well as they do in simulations."

Soon a second robot, to be called Nacho, will be helping develop that tech.

Lu says that should speed up their development process and ensure their software can run on different machines.

And, of course, provide Freddo with some company.

Gaming_Tech.title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
Gaming_Tech.text:
King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.

Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending.

Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.

It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn.

Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.

The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind".

He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone".

"Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.

Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.

He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution".

The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added.

But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them.

"The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates.

Sarah Friar, OpenAI's chief financial officer, said AI had the potential to solve some of society's "hardest problems" - but agreed its growing capabilities raised questions about safety and "how we ensure it always serves people".

"We need to address those questions together," she said.

"No one company or government can do that alone and I'm grateful to His Majesty for convening this discussion at such an important moment."

Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry.

The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact.

In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face.

After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity.

He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance.

The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe.

Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control.

Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.

Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight.

Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax".

Additional reporting by Philippa Wain

Gaming_Tech.title: Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity?
Gaming_Tech.text:
A slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action to slow the technology's development.

Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells.

Major developers OpenAI and Anthropic are urging lawmakers to regulate AI, with Microsoft's AI boss the latest to say rules are needed to prevent a "silicon species" from eventually competing with humanity.

But some have dismissed the calls as an effort by big AI developers to cement their dominance over rivals.

Regardless, the high profile claims have caused concern - here's what we know.

Some AI researchers say there are worrying signs of systems developing in their capabilities and power too quickly.

Evan Hubinger, made headlines with his belief that there is a greater than 10% chance AI "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

He works in alignment, a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI - essentially keeping it on track with what humans value.

While he said the risk from current systems was "low", his comments came as another researcher quit Anthropic and warned those developing the tech were losing their grip on it.

Jacob Coxon told the BBC he and other staff were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

These concerns are the latest in a long line of fears about AI's potential to threaten humanity should it grow to match or surpass human abilities.

Such worries date back decades, with Alan Turing writing in the 1950s that should intelligent machines become possible, they could take control.

In the last few years, major AI companies have been racing to develop increasingly capable systems, both for profit and in pursuit of creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans.

Unlike the systems and tools many people use daily to complete tasks like writing emails or generating videos, super intelligent AI systems should be able to handle far more complex tasks.

OpenAI and Anthropic say they aim to advance such tech in a way which benefits humans and protect them from its existential risks.

But some critics believe machines can never truly match humans. They say AI firms exaggerate the tech's abilities to boost their prominence or profit.

AI researchers, experts and bosses worried about the technology's potential to endanger humanity have outlined unsettling scenarios.

Dario Amodei wrote in September, external it had advanced "drastically faster" than expected, including in its "ability to build the next generation of AI".

This is the concern that AI, after it has reached a certain point, could theoretically begin improving itself without human involvement.

Such fears were sparked after a recent incident saw AI tools hack into websites, despite not being asked to.

Some concerned researchers have said those at the heart of its development are increasingly fearful about losing control of systems known as "AI agents".

These are tools given the ability to execute tasks and actions independently.

Other scenarios have included highly intelligent AI systems being used to amplify or lead espionage, cyber-attacks or biological warfare, or disrupt economies - whether by accident or design.

However, such warnings are prophetic, hypothetical and, for some, complete hyperbole, external.

Some experts have also criticised focusing on existential risks instead of those already playing out - such as image generation tools being to used create non-consensual nude deepfakes of women, misinform people and amplify scams.

A cross-party group of MPs and peers has published a report outlining human rights risks posed by AI, saying new laws are needed to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.

Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, have both called for regulation and a "slowdown" of the tech's development.

It is not the first time bosses or wider industry voices have clamoured for such action.

But questions have continued to mount over what any sort of "slowdown" - also backed by SpaceX boss Elon Musk - would actually look like.

Amodei said it would not mean "halting model training or technical progress".

Instead, he wants firms to "take adequate time" to safeguard the AI they are developing, and to ask for "third party evaluators" to check their work.

In a post on X, external, Altman said there was a need to pace development but added "when we talk about 'pacing' we do not mean 'stopping'."

"Progress has been rapid and will continue to be," he said.

"But it should be slower than it otherwise could be - interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs."

The OpenAI co-founder also said companies did not - and would not - wait for governments to act.

Altman later told attendees at a Salesforce conference people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe.

China had kept quiet in response to the wave of dire warnings from researchers at US companies.

In the face of fierce competition and limitations on its access to US components and chips being used to build AI infrastructure, the country has spurred homegrown development of the technology.

At the same time, it has called for greater global governance of AI.

The roll out of capable, open-source AI systems and tools by Chinese labs has shaken Western markets and developers in recent years.

Amodei warned in calling for a slowdown of AI development that China's progress and proficiency in AI would create national security risks for the US.

The Chinese foreign ministry criticised the comments, calling them narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition that served no one's interest.
